3.1|How is administrative formalism defined within Riggs' Prismatic-Sala framework?|The strict adherence of public officials to formal rules and legal codes in every administrative action.|The degree of divergence between official formal regulations and the actual practices of public administrators.|The complete absence of written constitutions, administrative laws, and formal institutions in a developing nation.|The process of converting informal traditional norms into legally binding statutory regulations.|Option B|Formalism describes the gap or discrepancy between formal written laws or policy mandates and the actual real-world behavior and implementation by administrators.
3.1|In a prismatic society, what does the key feature of overlapping signify regarding administrative structures?|Modern formal structures are established, but traditional social, political, and family structures continue to heavily influence administrative decisions.|Public agencies duplicate identical administrative functions to ensure structural redundancy and administrative efficiency.|Legislative bodies completely absorb the executive branch, eliminating the legal separation of powers.|Private corporations replace public sector bureaus in delivering essential social services.|Option A|Overlapping occurs when newly created modern administrative institutions exist on paper, yet informal traditional structures such as kinship, tribal loyalty, and nepotism continue to dominate actual decision-making.
3.1|According to Riggs, why is the administrative unit in a Prismatic Society termed the Sala rather than a Bureau or Chamber?|Because the Sala operates strictly under Weberian rational-legal principles of complete neutrality.|Because the administrative office is influenced by non-administrative factors such as family ties, favoritism, and clientelism.|Because the Sala represents a fully fused administrative structure devoid of functional differentiation.|Because public administrators in the Sala are selected exclusively through open competitive examinations.|Option B|The Sala corresponds to the administrative office in a prismatic society where rational-legal norms are undermined by clientelism, nepotism, and personal interests.
3.1|Where does the Prismatic model sit on Fred Riggs' structural-functional continuum between Fused and Diffracted societies?|At the extreme start of the continuum representing highly traditional, undifferentiated agricultural societies.|At the intermediate position representing developing societies undergoing rapid transition and partial differentiation.|At the end of the continuum representing fully industrialized and functionally specialized nations.|Completely outside the continuum as an isolated model inapplicable to administrative analysis.|Option B|The prismatic society occupies the middle state on the continuum between the fused (undifferentiated/traditional) and diffracted (highly differentiated/modern) societies.
3.1|A public administrator in a developing nation publicly champions merit-based recruitment laws but systematically hires family members for civil service positions. Which prismatic characteristics are directly demonstrated here?|High diffracted specialization and absolute functional specificity.|Complete lack of structural differentiation and total administrative fusion.|Formalism and overlapping through clientelism and nepotism.|Complete elimination of informal social influences in public administration.|Option C|Publicly upholding merit laws while practicing nepotism displays formalism (law vs. reality) and overlapping (family loyalties penetrating formal administrative processes).
3.1|Which statement accurately contrasts the level of functional differentiation in Riggs' Agraria and Industria models?|Agraria exhibits high functional differentiation, whereas Industria exhibits low functional differentiation.|Agraria exhibits low functional differentiation with multipurpose structures, whereas Industria exhibits high functional differentiation with specialized structures.|Both Agraria and Industria possess identical levels of functional differentiation and administrative specialization.|Neither Agraria nor Industria contains functional structures to perform administrative duties.|Option B|Agraria features low functional differentiation where a single structure performs multiple roles, while Industria features high differentiation with specialized institutions for distinct tasks.
3.1|Which outcome is most likely to occur in a public sector administration characterized by a high degree of prismatic formalism?|Administrative decisions will flawlessly align with official constitutional provisions and legal guidelines.|Comprehensive environmental policies will be enacted into law but largely ignored or unenforced in practice.|Public officials will lose all discretionary authority due to rigid automated regulatory monitoring.|Bureaucratic procedures will become entirely standardized across all regional government offices.|Option B|High formalism implies that while impressive and modern laws are passed, their actual implementation and compliance in practice remain exceptionally weak or non-existent.
3.1|What was Fred Riggs' primary objective in formulating the Prismatic Society and Sala Model for Development Administration?|To demonstrate that Western administrative theories can be applied without modification to developing countries.|To provide a contextual framework for understanding administrative behavior in non-Western, developing societies.|To argue that traditional agrarian societies are superior in efficiency to modern industrial societies.|To prove that formal legal reforms automatically guarantee economic development and political stability.|Option B|Riggs developed the Prismatic Society model to explain why Western administrative theories failed in developing nations due to unique ecological, socio-cultural, and structural dynamics.

11.1|Which administrative mechanism is typically most critical for a developmental state to effectively implement its industrial planning policies?|An insulated, highly competent, and meritocratic bureaucratic apparatus capable of long-term strategic planning|A decentralized administrative structure where local communities independently decide national economic policy|A completely randomized rotation of administrative personnel to prevent any long-term policy consistency|A political system that changes administrative priorities annually based on fluctuating public opinion polls|Option A|A competent, merit-based, and politically insulated bureaucracy is essential for a developmental state to formulate and execute long-term industrial policies without succumbing to short-term political pressures.
11.1|What is a primary objective of horizontal revenue allocation formulas in a federal system?|To ensure that all sub-national units receive an identical absolute amount of money regardless of their population size|To penalize economically disadvantaged regions and reward wealthy regions for high productivity|To address fiscal imbalances and ensure equity among sub-national units with varying capacities and developmental needs|To transfer all national revenue directly to the central government's executive reserve account|Option C|Horizontal revenue allocation formulas are designed to balance fiscal disparities among different sub-national units, accounting for differences in population, poverty levels, and revenue generation capacity.
11.1|Why did the economic models of the East Asian Tigers attract significant academic interest in development administration?|They demonstrated that rapid industrialization could be successfully engineered through strategic state intervention rather than pure market reliance|They proved that traditional agricultural societies could modernize solely by abolishing central government bureaucracies|They showed that foreign aid alone is sufficient to achieve sustained economic independence without domestic planning|They established that complete economic isolation from global markets is the most effective path to prosperity|Option A|The success of the East Asian Tigers challenged orthodox free-market views by proving that targeted state intervention and strategic industrial planning can generate extraordinary economic growth.
11.1|In intergovernmental fiscal negotiations, what does vertical fiscal imbalance typically refer to?|A situation where local governments generate more tax revenue than the central government can manage|The mismatch between the revenue-raising responsibilities and the expenditure obligations assigned to different tiers of government|A permanent legal dispute over the boundary lines separating neighboring federating states|The inability of private banks to provide loans to municipal administrative departments|Option B|Vertical fiscal imbalance occurs when lower tiers of government are assigned heavy expenditure responsibilities without having adequate independent revenue-raising powers, necessitating federal transfers.

Goswami is recognized as having coined the term development administration in 1955, which was subsequently popularized by scholars like Edward Weidner and Fred Riggs.
1.1|How does Edward Weidner primarily conceptualize development administration in terms of its core orientation?|An action-oriented and goal-oriented administrative system designed to drive socio-economic progress|A bureaucratic mechanism focused strictly on maintaining legal compliance and institutional stability|An academic sub-discipline dedicated exclusively to comparative legislative frameworks|A centralized fiscal model prioritizing strict budget adherence over project outcomes|Option A|Edward Weidner defined development administration as an action-oriented and goal-oriented system aimed at achieving socio-economic transformation and national progress.
1.1|According to Fred Riggs, development administration encompasses a dual focus involving which two primary components?|Tax collection efficiency and military logistics management|The administration of development programs and the continuous development of administrative capabilities|Democratic electoral reform and judicial independence enhancement|International trade regulation and diplomatic negotiation protocols|Option B|Fred Riggs famously conceptualized development administration as a two-way relationship involving both the execution of development programs and the strengthening of administrative capabilities.

1.1|How does a traditional public administration model fundamentally differ from development administration regarding its core institutional purpose?|Traditional administration prioritizes status-quo maintenance and law-and-order, whereas development administration focuses on planned change and results|Traditional administration is driven by private market incentives, whereas development administration relies solely on public funding|Traditional administration focuses exclusively on rural development, whereas development administration handles urban infrastructure|Traditional administration operates without bureaucratic hierarchy, whereas development administration is strictly rule-bound|Option A|Traditional administration historically centered on regulation, law and order, and preserving the status quo, whereas development administration is inherently oriented toward change, innovation, and results.

1.1|Which of the following scholars is most closely associated with defining development administration as a process geared toward implementing government-sponsored socio-economic plans and projects?|Max Weber|Edward Weidner|Woodrow Wilson|Frederick Taylor|Option B|Edward Weidner extensively emphasized the purposive, goal-seeking nature of public agencies engaged in driving socio-economic development plans.
1.1|In the context of the historical evolution of public administration, why was traditional public administration found inadequate for newly independent nations emerging after World War II?|It possessed too many technological tools for modern data analysis|It was primarily designed for maintenance of order and revenue collection rather than aggressive socio-economic engineering|It lacked any formal hierarchy or organizational structure|It focused entirely on economic privatization rather than state capacity|Option B|Newly decolonized nations required administrative systems capable of dynamic socio-economic transformation, which traditional law-and-order bureaucracies were not structured to provide.
1.1|Which conceptual element best distinguishes Fred Riggs' perspective on administrative development within the broader framework of development administration?|The complete elimination of bureaucratic red tape across government branches|The growth and strengthening of administrative capabilities to successfully execute complex programs|The reduction of public sector employment to favor private enterprise|The decentralization of military command structures to local municipalities|Option B|Fred Riggs emphasized that administrative development refers specifically to expanding and strengthening the internal capabilities and operational competencies of administrative systems.
15.1|Which of the following best defines privatization in the context of public enterprise reforms?|Reorganizing state enterprises to operate profitably without government treasury subsidies while maintaining complete state ownership|Divesting government equity shares and transferring management control to the private sector|Establishing state monopolies to completely control national strategic industries and market tariffs|Nationalizing private commercial sectors to expand state welfare programs and employment opportunities|Option B|Privatization involves the transfer of government equity shares and management responsibilities to private sector entities, distinguishing it from commercialization.
15.1|What is the defining characteristic of commercialization in public enterprises?|Operating for profit without treasury subsidies while retaining 100 percent state ownership|Transferring all voting shares and board governance entirely to private investors|Dissolving the enterprise completely to liquidate remaining assets for public debt repayment|Subsidizing consumer goods directly through mandatory government price ceilings|Option A|Commercialization focuses on reorganizing state enterprises to function efficiently for profit without reliance on government treasury subsidies while keeping ownership entirely in state hands.

15.1|When a state enterprise is commercialized, what happens to its ownership structure?|It is entirely split among foreign venture capitalists and multinational conglomerates|It remains 100 percent owned by the government while adopting commercial business practices|It is converted into a cooperative worker-owned enterprise with no state oversight|It is divided equally between municipal governments and private retail shareholders|Option B|Commercialization modernizes the operational framework of a public enterprise while preserving complete 100 percent government ownership.
15.1|What is a typical consequence for the workforce when public enterprises undergo aggressive privatization?|Mass retrenchment and workforce down-sizing to maximize private corporate efficiency|Mandatory wage increases and lifetime employment guarantees for all personnel|Immediate transition of all operational staff into high-ranking cabinet ministers|Automatic promotion of manual laborers to executive board directors|Option A|Privatization frequently results in employee retrenchment as private new owners restructure operations to reduce costs and enhance productivity.
15.1|How does privatization fundamentally differ from commercialization regarding asset distribution?|Privatization divests government equity shares to private actors whereas commercialization retains full state ownership|Privatization nationalizes private assets whereas commercialization sells all assets to foreign governments|Commercialization eliminates enterprise assets entirely whereas privatization builds new public infrastructure|Commercialization transfers equity to private holders whereas privatization keeps equity within the treasury|Option A|The core distinction is that privatization transfers equity and management to private actors, whereas commercialization keeps ownership within the state.

15.1|Why might a government choose commercialization instead of outright privatization?|To retain direct control and ownership of strategic sectors while eliminating financial burdens on the treasury|To completely rid the public sector of any responsibility for infrastructure development|To instantly transfer all operational financial risks to private foreign banks|To bypass regulatory oversight and avoid consumer protection laws permanently|Option A|Commercialization allows the state to stop draining public funds via treasury subsidies while still holding onto strategic public enterprises.

5.1|In the context of the socio-cultural ecology of development administration, how can ethnic pluralism impact state institutions?|It guarantees uniform compliance with centralized administrative policies across all regions|It eliminates cultural friction by blending all minority groups into a single administrative class|It can introduce competing loyalties and pressures that complicate national unity, equitable resource allocation, and bureaucratic neutrality|It forces the state to abandon modern bureaucratic structures in favor of tribal councils|Option C|Ethnic pluralism often brings diverse cultural demands and loyalties into the public sphere, creating unique challenges for administrators striving for impartial and unified policy delivery.
5.1|How do extended family pressures typically manifest as an ecological force within developing administrative systems?|By encouraging strict adherence to meritocratic recruitment and impersonal bureaucratic rules|By blurring the boundaries between public office and private obligations through demands for preferential treatment or jobs|By forcing public officials to relocate frequently to distant provinces to avoid local bias|By eliminating traditional social support networks in favor of state-run welfare systems|Option B|Extended family pressures in traditional or transitional societies often create conflicts of interest, where public officials face strong social expectations to favor relatives in employment or resource distribution.
5.1|What is a primary administrative implication of political instability and fragile democratic institutions in a developing nation?|Policy continuity and long-term administrative planning are frequently disrupted by shifting political regimes|Bureaucracies automatically become completely autonomous and immune to political interference|Public officials gain absolute permanent tenure that can never be altered by any regime change|Development projects are executed with total predictability because laws change daily|Option A|Political instability and weak democratic frameworks create an unpredictable environment where administrative priorities, funding, and leadership shift constantly, disrupting long-term development.
5.1|Which economic indicator is most commonly analyzed to understand the resource capacity and general financial health of a developing state within its administrative ecology?|The national literacy rate and primary school enrollment percentages|The Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and national debt levels|The total number of registered non-governmental organizations in urban centers|The average annual rainfall and agricultural export tonnage|Option B|GDP and national debt are fundamental macroeconomic indicators that dictate the fiscal space, borrowing capacity, and resource mobilization potential of a development administration.
5.1|How do civic attitudes and political culture shape the practice of development administration?|They dictate whether citizens view public officials as accountable public servants or distant rulers, influencing public participation and compliance|They have zero impact because administrative systems operate entirely independently of public perception|They solely determine the architectural layout and physical security measures of government ministry buildings|They regulate the international exchange rates and foreign direct investment inflows directly|Option A|Civic attitudes shape how citizens interact with the state, establishing the baseline for public trust, civic engagement, cooperation, and the legitimacy of administrative programs.
5.1|Why is economic debt considered a critical ecological constraint for public administration in developing countries?|It requires the state to dedicate a massive portion of national revenues to debt servicing, starving public administration of operational funds|It completely prevents the government from collecting any domestic taxes from its citizens|It forces the administrative system to focus entirely on military defense rather than public works|It automatically transforms a command economy into a pure market capitalism overnight|Option A|High national debt burdens restrict fiscal policy flexibility, forcing governments to cut administrative budgets and compromise public service delivery to meet debt obligations.
5.1|Which statement accurately contrasts political stability with political instability in relation to administrative efficiency?|Political stability fosters predictable policy implementation and institutional memory, whereas political instability causes frequent administrative purges and policy reversals|Political stability creates stagnant bureaucracies that never adapt, while instability forces rapid modernization|Political stability guarantees total corruption, while instability eradicates all forms of bureaucratic patronage|Political stability has no effect on administration, whereas instability ensures maximum citizen participation|Option A|Stable political environments allow development agencies to build institutional capacity and see long-term projects to completion, whereas instability leads to constant disruption and turnover.
5.1|Within the framework of administrative ecology, what does the term socio-cultural pluralism primarily encompass within a developing nation?|The existence of multiple distinct ethnic, linguistic, religious, or tribal groups within a single state boundary|The presence of competing economic theories within the central bank's advisory board|The division of administrative power between the executive, legislative, and judicial branches|The coexistence of multiple political parties competing in national elections|Option A|Socio-cultural pluralism refers to the societal diversity arising from multiple ethnic, linguistic, or religious groups, which profoundly influences administrative dynamics and state-society relations.

15.1|Which of the following best defines privatization in the context of public enterprise reforms?|Reorganizing state enterprises to operate strictly for profit without treasury subsidies while retaining total government ownership|Divesting government equity shares and transferring management control to the private sector|Eliminating all forms of government oversight while maintaining full state ownership of enterprise assets|Transitioning a public agency into a non-governmental organization dependent entirely on foreign grants|Option B|Privatization involves the complete or partial transfer of government equity shares and management control to private sector entities.
15.1|What is the core distinguishing feature of commercialization compared to privatization?|Commercialization transfers total asset ownership to private shareholders while retaining public management|Commercialization reorganizes state enterprises to operate for profit without treasury subsidies while retaining 100 percent state ownership|Commercialization completely abolishes government regulation and exposes the enterprise to immediate foreign takeover|Commercialization relies entirely on direct funding and annual budgetary allocations from the national treasury|Option B|Commercialization mandates that state enterprises operate profitably and independently of government subventions while remaining wholly owned by the state.
15.1|Which of the following is considered a primary socioeconomic risk associated with the privatization of public enterprises?|Guaranteed long-term employment security for all existing public sector workers|Significant tariff hikes and potential risks of private monopolies exploiting consumers|Immediate elimination of wealth concentration and a more equitable distribution of national assets|Complete eradication of market inefficiencies through mandatory price controls set by the state|Option B|Privatization can lead to severe market distortions, including high tariffs and the emergence of private monopolies that lack competitive checks.
15.1|When a state-owned enterprise is commercialized, how is its financial relationship with the government fundamentally altered?|It continues to rely exclusively on unconditional annual grants and treasury subsidies for operational survival|It becomes completely tax-exempt and no longer contributes any financial dividends to the national treasury|It must operate commercially for profit, eliminating its dependence on continuous treasury subsidies|It is legally prohibited from charging market-driven prices for its goods and services|Option C|Commercialization requires public enterprises to become self-sustaining business entities that generate profits instead of depending on government subventions.
15.1|Which challenge is most commonly cited regarding the social impact of structural public enterprise reforms on the workforce?|Mass retrenchment and job losses as private owners streamline operations for efficiency|Immediate and permanent wage increases across all operational tiers of the enterprise|The mandatory unionization of all incoming private sector shareholders and board members|A guaranteed transition of all civil servants into lifetime diplomatic postings|Option A|Enterprise reforms often trigger substantial workforce reductions or retrenchments as management cuts costs to maximize profitability.
15.1|In analyzing asset concentration during public enterprise reforms, what is the primary concern for regulatory authorities?|The dispersion of small shares among millions of rural citizens leading to corporate micro-management|The accumulation of critical national infrastructure and wealth into the hands of a few private entities|The total absence of any private buyers willing to acquire government shares|The excessive fragmentation of corporate ownership preventing any unified strategic direction|Option B|Asset concentration poses a major threat because vital economic resources can become monopolized by a small elite or powerful corporate conglomerates.
15.1|What administrative action is legally and structurally necessary to achieve true privatization of a government corporation?|Transferring management authority and divesting government equity stakes to private investors|Revising the national budget to increase annual capital allocations and operational subventions|Converting the enterprise into a fully funded ministerial department under direct bureaucratic rule|Granting the civil service commission direct control over the daily appointment of executive directors|Option A|True privatization requires shifting both ownership equity and management control out of government hands and into the private sector.
15.1|Why might a government choose commercialization instead of outright privatization for a strategic national utility?|To completely divest all state financial risk and distance the government from infrastructure management|To retain 100 percent state ownership while forcing the utility to adopt efficient, profit-driven business practices|To permanently subsidize consumer costs using unlimited revenue drawn directly from the national treasury|To eliminate all regulatory oversight and allow the utility to operate without accountability|Option B|Commercialization allows governments to maintain strategic control and 100 percent ownership while enforcing operational efficiency and financial self-sufficiency.
15.1|Which outcome is a direct consequence of eliminating treasury subsidies for a commercialized state enterprise?|The enterprise is forced to optimize revenue generation and cost management to survive financially|The enterprise must immediately dissolve and liquidate all physical assets to repay national debts|The government automatically assumes all commercial liabilities and operational debts incurred by the firm|The enterprise transitions into a charitable foundation dependent on public donations|Option A|Removing treasury subsidies compels the enterprise to rely entirely on its own commercial revenues and sound financial management.
15.1|Which of the following problems represents a critical governance challenge when public monopolies are transferred to private hands without adequate regulation?|The creation of a hyper-competitive market with too many overlapping private service providers|The exploitation of consumers through unchecked pricing power and monopolistic abuse|The immediate decentralization of corporate decision-making down to local municipal councils|The elimination of all profit motives in favor of absolute public welfare maximization|Option B|Unregulated private monopolies can exploit consumers through steep tariff hikes and poor service quality because consumers lack alternative choices.

11.1|What role do revenue allocation formulas play in managing center-periphery fiscal tensions in federations?|They provide a structured and institutionalized mechanism to distribute national wealth and mitigate resource conflicts|They allow the central government to arbitrarily confiscate regional treasuries without legal oversight|They completely erase economic disparities between urban centers and rural farming communities instantly|They serve as a symbolic gesture with no real impact on the operational budgets of subnational governments|Option A|Structured revenue allocation formulas help balance fiscal power and ease tensions between central and subnational governments by transparently sharing national wealth.
11.1|Why is industrial planning considered a cornerstone of the developmental state model?|Because it allows the state to strategically select and nurture competitive export-oriented industries|Because it prevents any form of technological advancement from disrupting traditional handicrafts|Because it ensures that all manufacturing output is entirely consumed within local rural markets|Because it prohibits private enterprises from participating in any sector of the national economy|Option A|Industrial planning enables the government to coordinate investments and support targeted industries to build global market competitiveness.
11.1|Which factor frequently intensifies derivation debates during intergovernmental fiscal negotiations?|Disparities between resource-rich regions demanding higher retention and resource-poor regions advocating for equality|Unanimous agreement among all regional governors regarding the absolute irrelevance of natural resources|The complete absence of any revenue generated from natural resource extraction across the entire federation|A constitutional ban on the collection of personal income taxes by any tier of government|Option A|Derivation debates are fueled by the tension between resource-rich regions wanting a greater share of their earnings and resource-poor regions emphasizing needs-based sharing.
11.1|What distinguishes the interventionist approach of a developmental state from socialist command economies?|The developmental state actively collaborates with and guides private capital rather than completely abolishing private property|The developmental state completely outlaws market transactions and relies entirely on centralized rationing|The developmental state refuses to engage in any form of long-term economic planning or forecasting|The developmental state focuses exclusively on agricultural production while ignoring all manufacturing sectors|Option A|Unlike command economies that abolish private ownership, developmental states work alongside and guide private enterprise toward national economic goals.
11.1|Which administrative capability is most critical for a government successfully executing a developmental state model?|A highly competent and insulated bureaucratic apparatus capable of implementing complex industrial policies|A completely decentralized administrative structure where local villages make independent monetary policies|A loose regulatory framework that permits widespread corruption and rent-seeking behaviors among officials|An elected legislature that alters economic plans annually based on fluctuating public moods|Option A|A skilled, professional, and relatively autonomous bureaucracy is essential for effectively planning and executing long-term developmental strategies.

15.1|What is a typical financial implication of successfully commercializing a public enterprise?|Increased dependence on annual government subventions and treasury bailouts|Complete financial self-sufficiency and operation for profit without treasury subsidies|Mandatory liquidation of all corporate assets to fund local municipal projects|Immediate suspension of all revenue collection from consumers and businesses|Option B|Successful commercialization frees the enterprise from treasury dependence, enabling it to generate its own profits and sustain operations independently.

3.1|What does Riggs mean by the concept of formalism within the context of a prismatic society?|The strict enforcement of written laws without exception|The complete absence of any legal or administrative framework|The vast discrepancy between prescribed written laws and actual behavioral realities|The harmonization of traditional customs with modern bureaucratic mandates|Option C|Formalism occurs when laws, rules, and constitutions exist on paper but hold little practical sway over actual behavior and governance.
3.1|What is the administrative subsystem of the prismatic society called in Riggs's theoretical framework?|The Apparatus|The Sala|The Bureau|The Directorate|Option B|Riggs coined the term Sala to describe the specific administrative structure of a prismatic society, lying between the chamber of traditional governments and the modern bureau.

3.1|In Riggs's prismatic model, what causes administrative behavior to be heavily influenced by family and religious ties rather than official duties?|Overlapping|Heterogeneity|Formalism|Differentiation|Option A|Overlapping refers to the condition where administrative structures fail to differentiate, allowing primary ties like family and religion to dominate official work.

3.1|What does the term heterogeneity signify in the context of Fred Riggs's Prismatic model?|The complete absence of formal laws in developing countries|The simultaneous existence of modern urban practices alongside primitive traditional methods|The strict separation of political affairs from administrative duties|The absolute dominance of achievement-based recruitment over nepotism|Option B|Heterogeneity refers to the concurrent presence of highly modernized institutions and deeply entrenched traditional or primitive methods within developing prismatic societies.
3.1|In Riggs's framework, what is meant by administrative formalism?|The complete alignment between written constitutional laws and actual societal behavior|The total absence of any written legal frameworks in a transitional state|The gap or discrepancy between prescribed legal rules and actual administrative practices|The strict enforcement of meritocratic recruitment policies in a bureaucratic agency|Option C|Formalism occurs when official laws, rules, and structures bear little resemblance to how things are actually practiced and carried out in reality.
3.1|What is the defining characteristic of the Sala model within a prismatic society?|A clear separation between political authority and administrative execution|A total reliance on meritocracy and universalistic promotion criteria|The overlapping of formal administrative structures with informal family and clan loyalties|The elimination of clientelism and nepotism in public service delivery|Option C|The Sala model represents the prismatic office where formal administrative structures overlap with traditional patterns of nepotism, clientelism, and family influence.
3.1|Which phenomenon is most likely to thrive within an overlapping administrative system like the Sala?|Impartial policy implementation based strictly on objective merit|Strict adherence to meritocratic civil service examinations without outside interference|Nepotism and clientelism driven by overlapping modern and traditional loyalties|Complete structural differentiation between economic and political institutions|Option C|Overlapping allows traditional kinship ties, nepotism, and clientelism to infiltrate formal bureaucratic structures, compromising neutral administration.

What concept does this illustrate?|Formalism|Agrarian purity|Heterogeneity|The Industria ideal type|Option C|Heterogeneity captures this exact duality, where modern technology and advanced systems coexist side-by-side with primitive or traditional methods.

15.1|Which of the following is a major socio-economic challenge commonly associated with privatization?|Guaranteed long-term job security for all existing public sector workers|The elimination of all market competition leading to state-run monopolies|The risk of creating private monopolies and subsequent tariff hikes for consumers|Immediate reduction in consumer prices due to increased private efficiency|Option C|Privatization often carries the risk of replacing public monopolies with private ones, which can lead to negative consumer outcomes like tariff hikes.
15.1|How does commercialization fundamentally differ from privatization regarding ownership?|Commercialization transfers all assets to private shareholders while privatization keeps assets public|Commercialization maintains 100 percent state ownership whereas privatization divests government equity|Commercialization involves joint-venture partnerships with foreign governments exclusively|Privatization retains state ownership of all shares while commercialization sells them off|Option B|Commercialization reorganizes the enterprise while retaining 100 percent state ownership, whereas privatization divests government equity to the private sector.
15.1|Which negative outcome is typically feared by labor unions when public enterprises undergo privatization or commercialization?|Massive retrenchment and workforce reduction to cut operational costs|Immediate salary increases for all remaining administrative staff|Mandatory promotion of junior workers to executive positions|Total decentralization of management to regional worker councils|Option A|Retrenchment or downsizing is a common restructuring measure taken by new private or commercialized management to optimize labor efficiency.
15.1|What is a primary financial objective of commercializing a state-owned enterprise?|To rely permanently on annual budgetary allocations from the national treasury|To eliminate the need for treasury subsidies through profitable self-sufficiency|To maximize tax revenues by imposing heavy fines on citizens|To accumulate foreign debt through international bond markets|Option B|Commercialization aims to make public enterprises financially self-sufficient and profitable so they no longer drain public funds via treasury subsidies.
15.1|Asset concentration is frequently cited as a negative consequence of privatization because it tends to...|distribute wealth evenly among all tax-paying citizens|concentrate economic power and ownership into the hands of a wealthy few|prevent private investors from buying more than one share|force corporations to split into smaller worker cooperatives|Option C|Asset concentration occurs when privatized assets are bought up by a small elite or wealthy class, exacerbating economic inequality.
15.1|When a state enterprise is commercialized, who retains the ultimate equity ownership of the institution?|Private domestic investors and institutional shareholders|Foreign multinational conglomerates and international banks|The central government through 100 percent state ownership|The executive labor union representing the workers|Option C|A core principle of commercialization is that the state retains 100 percent ownership of the enterprise while altering its operational management style.
15.1|Which of the following represents a direct strategic shift during the privatization of a public utility?|Moving from a profit-driven model to a purely social welfare service model|Transferring equity shares and operational management control from the state to private investors|Abolishing all user fees to provide free services to the entire population|Increasing the reliance on government administrative ministries for daily oversight|Option B|Privatization involves transferring both equity shares and management control away from the government to private sector entities.
15.1|Why might a commercialized public enterprise still face public scrutiny regarding tariff hikes?|Because they must generate profits without government subsidies, compelling them to price services economically realistically|Because government ministries legally dictate maximum price ceilings below production costs|Because private shareholders demand immediate dividend payouts from public funds|Because commercialized entities are prohibited by law from charging any fees for services|Option A|To operate without treasury subsidies and achieve profitability, commercialized enterprises often have to adjust tariffs to reflect true operational costs.

3.1|Which of the following best characterizes the Agraria model in Fred Riggs' comparative typology?|A modern industrial economy driven by achievement criteria|A traditional society characterized by ascribed status and an agricultural base|A transitional society experiencing high institutional overlap|A bureaucratic system dominated by formal laws and universalism|Option B|The Agraria model represents traditional societies where social status is determined by ascription and economic activity is primarily agricultural.
3.1|What defines the Industria model in the structural-functional approach of Fred Riggs?|Widespread nepotism and clientelism within the administrative apparatus|High functional specialization achievement-oriented norms and industrialization|A wide discrepancy between written administrative laws and actual bureaucratic behavior|The coexistence of highly modern technology alongside primitive economic practices|Option B|The Industria model describes modern, highly differentiated societies characterized by universalism, achievement orientation, and industrial production.
3.1|How does Fred Riggs describe the transitional societies that fall between traditional Agraria and modern Industria?|The Prismatic model|The Bureaucratic model|The Classical model|The Neoliberal model|Option A|Riggs used the Prismatic model to analyze transitional societies that exhibit characteristics of both traditional and modern systems.
3.1|What core feature of the Prismatic society involves the simultaneous presence of highly modern systems alongside primitive or traditional practices?|Formalism|Overlap|Heterogeneity|Ascription|Option C|Heterogeneity refers to the simultaneous existence of deeply contrasting systems, such as advanced urban technology operating alongside primitive rural methods.
3.1|In the context of Riggs' Prismatic model, what does the concept of formalism describe?|The complete integration of traditional values into modern industrial machinery|The absolute alignment between constitutional mandates and administrative reality|A significant discrepancy between prescribed written laws and actual administrative practices|The strict enforcement of meritocratic recruitment in bureaucratic agencies|Option C|Formalism occurs when laws and regulations look modern on paper but bear little resemblance to how things are actually practiced in reality.
3.1|What does the concept of overlapping signify within Riggs' Sala model of administration?|A clear separation between political authority and administrative execution|The dominance of specialized bureaucratic structures over political institutions|The failure of formal administrative structures to monopolize functions resulting in nepotism and family influence|The complete absence of informal social networks in modernizing states|Option C|Overlapping describes a condition in the Sala model where formal administrative structures fail to perform specialized roles, allowing family, clan, and political loyalties to dictate governance.
3.1|Which specific administrative model did Fred Riggs use to depict the bureaucracy of a prismatic society?|The Sala model|The Cabinet model|The Executive model|The Agrarian model|Option A|Riggs coined the term Sala to describe the typical bureaucratic structure of a prismatic society, reflecting a blend of traditional and modern administrative traits.
3.1|Why are administrative systems in transitional prismatic societies frequently prone to clientelism and nepotism?|Because universalistic recruitment criteria completely replace traditional values|Because administrative roles overlap heavily with traditional family and communal loyalties|Because formal laws are strictly enforced without any social deviation|Because industrial production completely eliminates agricultural influence|Option B|Overlapping structures mean that non-administrative criteria like family ties and political patronage heavily influence bureaucratic behavior in the Sala model.

13.1|What is a defining functional focus of the Developmental Theory of local government according to the module notes?|Acting as the primary coordinator of grassroots community development|Focusing exclusively on international trade policies|Centralizing all administrative power in the national capital|Dismantling public service delivery mechanisms|Option A|The Developmental Theory emphasizes the role of local government as the primary coordinator of grassroots community development.
13.1|Which of the following best contrasts the Democratic-Participatory Theory from the Efficient-Service Theory?|Participatory theory emphasizes civic engagement and leadership while efficient-service theory emphasizes service delivery efficiency|Participatory theory rejects elections while efficient-service theory mandates them|Participatory theory applies only to national states while efficient-service theory applies to villages|Participatory theory ignores citizens while efficient-service theory ignores administration|Option A|The primary distinction lies in Mill's focus on civic education and engagement versus Mackenzie and Sharpe's focus on service delivery efficiency.
13.1|A local government initiative designed to mobilize rural communities for infrastructural building projects falls most directly under which conceptual framework?|Democratic-Participatory Theory|Efficient-Service Theory|Developmental Theory|Classical Realist Theory|Option C|Mobilizing communities for grassroots infrastructural development aligns directly with the Developmental Theory's focus on community development coordination.
13.1|Which perspective highlights the value of local government units because they are better positioned to understand and respond to immediate local needs than a distant central government?|Efficient-Service Theory|Anarchist Collective Theory|Feudal Lordship Model|Monarchical Absolutism|Option A|The Efficient-Service Theory supports local governance because proximity allows for more responsive and efficient localized service delivery.
11.1|What characterizes the primary role of the state within the Developmental State Model?|A passive regulatory stance focused exclusively on maintaining law and order|An active interventionist and entrepreneurial role in industrial planning and capital formation|A complete reliance on market forces to dictate all national economic priorities|A strict policy of non-intervention and total economic deregulation|Option B|The developmental state model requires the state to take an active, interventionist, and entrepreneurial role in directing industrial planning and fostering capital formation.
11.1|Which group of economies is historically renowned as the classic examples of the Developmental State Model?|The Nordic Social Democracies|The East Asian Tigers including South Korea, Singapore, and Taiwan|The Latin American Import Substitution Industrialization pioneers|The post-Soviet transition economies of Eastern Europe|Option B|South Korea, Singapore, and Taiwan are classical exemplars of the East Asian Tigers that successfully applied the developmental state model.
11.1|What is the core function of a federation account sharing formula in intergovernmental fiscal relations?|To determine how collectively pooled public revenues are distributed among different tiers of government|To establish private sector corporate tax rates for multinational corporations|To regulate international trade tariffs between sovereign nations|To audit individual municipal government expenditures annually|Option A|A federation account sharing formula dictates how nationally collected revenues are shared across various tiers or levels of government within a federal system.
11.1|What is the central focus of derivation debates within intergovernmental fiscal frameworks?|Whether sub-national units should retain a higher proportion of revenue generated directly from resources within their borders|How to eliminate all forms of central government taxation entirely|The legal procedures for merging distinct regional administrative jurisdictions|The mechanisms for calculating foreign aid disbursements from international lenders|Option A|Derivation debates center around whether regions or states that produce specific resources should receive a larger share of the revenue derived from them.
11.1|Which institutional action best aligns with the operational strategy of a developmental state?|Dismantling all national industrial policies to favor unguided market competition|Targeting specific strategic industrial sectors for state-led investment and protection|Outsourcing all infrastructure development to foreign entities without state oversight|Abolishing central planning bodies to reduce bureaucratic capacity|Option B|Developmental states actively target and support strategic industries through state-led planning, subsidies, and investment to accelerate national economic growth.
11.1|How does the developmental state model primarily approach capital formation?|By depending solely on foreign direct investment without domestic interventions|Through aggressive state direction, strategic savings mobilization, and public investment coordination|By discouraging domestic savings in favor of consumer spending booms|By privatizing all banking and financial institutions immediately|Option B|Capital formation in developmental states is aggressively steered by the government through coordinated public investments, domestic savings policies, and targeted financial controls.
11.1|Why are intergovernmental fiscal relations a critical component of development administration?|They ensure absolute financial uniformity across all local municipalities without exception|They determine the fiscal capacity and resource autonomy of sub-national administrative units to deliver public goods|They eliminate the need for any administrative accountability mechanisms|They restrict public expenditure strictly to national defense portfolios|Option B|Intergovernmental fiscal relations directly shape how resources flow to different administrative tiers, affecting their capability to execute developmental mandates.
11.1|What distinguishes a developmental state from a purely laissez-faire capitalist state?|A total absence of private property rights within developmental economies|Direct state intervention and guidance in economic and industrial transformation rather than passive oversight|Exclusive reliance on agricultural exports as the sole driver of gross domestic product|The complete elimination of democratic governance structures|Option B|Unlike laissez-faire states that practice non-intervention, developmental states actively steer industrial transformation, resource allocation, and economic planning.
11.1|In the context of federation accounts, what typically triggers intense political and fiscal debate among constituent units?|Disagreements over the specific criteria and weightings used for revenue distribution formulas|The implementation of uniform national public holiday schedules|The standardization of civil service uniform designs across regions|The scheduling of routine census data collection intervals|Option A|Constituent units frequently contest the specific metrics used in sharing formulas, such as population, equality, land mass, and derivation principles.
11.1|What long-term objective motivated the institutional frameworks of the East Asian Tigers under the developmental model?|Rapid structural transformation and export-led industrialization through strategic state guidance|Achieving complete economic isolation from global trade networks|Transitioning entirely away from manufacturing toward subsistence farming|Dismantling state bureaucracy to establish a stateless society|Option A|The East Asian Tigers utilized state intervention to rapidly industrialize their economies and position themselves competitively in global export markets.
14.1|Which of the following best characterizes the core principle of Integrated Rural Development (IRD)?|A singular focus on agricultural production output|A multi-sectoral approach combining agriculture roads water and electrification|An exclusive reliance on multinational corporate social responsibility|A strategy centered entirely on urban industrial migration|Option B|Integrated Rural Development relies on a multi-sectoral strategy that simultaneously addresses foundational needs such as agriculture, infrastructure, water, and electrification.|
14.1|What is the primary function of community cooperatives in the context of rural development?|Directly setting macroeconomic monetary policies for the state|Enforcing strict environmental remediation laws on transnational corporations|Pooling community resources to provide micro-credit and facilitate produce marketing|Replacing local government administrative structures entirely|Option C|Community cooperatives empower rural populations by pooling resources together to offer accessible micro-credit and streamline the marketing of local agricultural produce.|
14.1|In the framework of rural development strategies, how do Transnational Corporations (TNCs) typically contribute to local sustainability?|Through government tax collection mandates and foreign trade tariffs|Through Corporate Social Responsibility initiatives and environmental remediation|By managing state-run public utility monopolies directly|By abolishing traditional community cooperative systems|Option B|Transnational corporations contribute to rural development efforts primarily through Corporate Social Responsibility programs and active environmental remediation projects.|
14.1|Why is a multi-sectoral approach considered essential in Integrated Rural Development strategies?|Because focusing solely on farming ignores vital infrastructure like roads and clean water access|Because it completely eliminates the need for any community cooperative involvement|Because it prevents transnational corporations from investing in rural zones|Because it shifts all administrative responsibilities exclusively to the private sector|Option A|Rural communities face interdependent challenges, meaning agricultural growth cannot succeed without concurrent investments in infrastructure like roads and water systems.|
14.1|How do community cooperatives primarily assist rural farmers with financial constraints?|By offering centralized commercial banking loans with high collateral requirements|By providing micro-credit facilities derived from pooled community resources|By funding large-scale international trade agreements|By absorbing all agricultural debt through government subsidies|Option B|Cooperatives overcome rural financial exclusion by establishing internal micro-credit systems funded through pooled member resources.|
14.1|What role does rural infrastructure development play within an Integrated Rural Development framework?|It serves as a secondary decorative enhancement with little economic impact|It acts as a critical multi-sectoral component enabling market access and resource distribution|It functions exclusively to facilitate urban commuter traffic|It replaces the need for agricultural training programs entirely|Option B|Infrastructure components like roads and electrification are critical multi-sectoral elements that enable market connectivity and enhance overall rural productivity.|
14.1|What is a key objective of produce marketing functions within community cooperatives?|To compete globally with state-owned industrial enterprises|To secure better market prices and bargaining power for smallholder farmers|To establish legal monopolies over national food distribution|To eliminate the private retail sector completely|Option C|Produce marketing through cooperatives helps small-scale farmers aggregate their yields to negotiate better prices and bypass exploitative intermediaries.|
14.1|How does environmental remediation by TNCs impact rural development areas?|By restoring degraded ecosystems and mitigating industrial ecological damage|By converting agricultural lands into heavy industrial manufacturing zones|By privatizing community water sources for corporate profit|By increasing carbon emissions to stimulate local heating infrastructure|Option A|Environmental remediation involves cleaning up and restoring polluted or degraded ecosystems, which safeguards the natural resource base of rural communities.|
14.1|Which combination of sectors best represents the scope of Integrated Rural Development?|Military defense aerospace technology and digital cryptocurrency|Agriculture rural infrastructure water supply and electrification|Stock market trading international diplomacy and luxury tourism|Urban real estate development corporate tax law and digital marketing|Option B|Integrated Rural Development explicitly coordinates multiple foundational sectors, specifically agriculture, roads, water supply, and electrification, to uplift rural regions.|
14.1|What is the primary motivation behind Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiatives implemented by TNCs in rural areas?|To fulfill statutory tax obligations owed directly to municipal authorities|To contribute positively to local community welfare and mitigate negative operational footprints|To take over complete sovereign administrative control of rural districts|To replace community cooperatives as the sole financial institution|Option B|Corporate Social Responsibility allows transnational corporations to invest back into local communities, supporting welfare and addressing environmental or social impacts.|
15.1|Which of the following best defines the privatization of state enterprises in development administration?|Transferring 100 percent equity shares to the private sector while maintaining government management control|Divesting government equity shares and transferring management responsibilities to the private sector|Reorganizing state-owned enterprises to operate strictly for profit without relying on treasury subsidies|Liquidating public assets permanently without transferring any operational roles to commercial entities|Option B|Privatization involves the complete or partial divesting of government equity shares and management control to private sector entities to improve efficiency.
15.1|What is the core structural distinction between commercialization and privatization in public enterprise reforms?|Commercialization eliminates all state ownership while privatization retains government shares|Commercialization maintains 100 percent state ownership while requiring profit-driven operation, whereas privatization transfers equity to the private sector|Commercialization relies entirely on treasury subsidies whereas privatization prohibits any government involvement|Commercialization transfers management to private hands while privatization keeps management within the civil service|Option B|Commercialization reorganizes state enterprises to run profitably without government subsidies while keeping 100 percent state ownership, unlike privatization which divests equity.
15.1|A state-owned utility company is restructured to operate on a strictly commercial, profit-making basis without receiving any further treasury subventions, though the government retains full ownership of all shares. This reform is an example of which of the following?|Privatization|Commercialization|Nationalization|Deregulation|Option B|This scenario describes commercialization, where a state enterprise operates for profit without treasury subsidies while retaining 100 percent state ownership.
15.1|Which of the following is a prominent socioeconomic challenge frequently associated with the privatization of public enterprises?|Complete elimination of market competition|Guaranteed reduction in consumer utility tariffs|Risk of creating private monopolies and severe asset concentration|Excessive accumulation of surplus revenue by the national treasury|Option C|Privatization often carries the risk of replacing public monopolies with private monopolies, leading to asset concentration and potential welfare losses.
15.1|When a developing nation implements public enterprise reforms through privatization, which outcome regarding the workforce is most commonly anticipated as a negative social consequence?|Immediate expansion of public sector employment benefits|Massive workforce retrenchment and job cuts to optimize efficiency|Guaranteed lifelong tenure for all existing civil servants|Decentralization of labor unions into autonomous worker cooperatives|Option B|Retrenchment is a major challenge during privatization as private owners typically streamline operations and cut surplus labor to maximize profitability.
15.1|Why might a government choose commercialization instead of privatization for a strategic national infrastructure asset?|To completely avoid any accountability to the legislature or public oversight|To eliminate all operational risks and transfer financial liabilities to international banks|To enforce profit-driven efficiency and eliminate treasury dependency while keeping ultimate public control|To immediately maximize short-term capital flight from the domestic economy|Option C|Commercialization allows the state to retain 100 percent ownership and control over strategic assets while forcing them to operate efficiently and independently of treasury subsidies.
15.1|Which of the following is a direct economic consequence often experienced by consumers following the privatization of essential utility services?|Sudden tariff hikes as private entities seek maximum return on investment|Mandatory price freezes imposed by international financial institutions|Permanent elimination of user fees across all socioeconomic strata|Universal provision of free commodities subsidized by private shareholders|Option A|Private entities prioritize profit maximization, which frequently leads to tariff hikes for consumers once state price controls are removed.
15.1|In the context of public enterprise reforms, what does the divestment of government equity shares primarily entail?|Increasing budgetary allocations from the national treasury to state corporations|Selling state-owned shares to private investors to reduce public sector footprints|Transferring administrative duties from lower-level ministries to the executive cabinet|Consolidating all public corporations into a single centralized government ministry|Option B|Divesting government equity shares means selling off state-owned ownership stakes to private investors, shifting control and financial risk.
15.1|Which of the following best describes the operational mandate of a fully commercialized state enterprise?|Operating as a nonprofit charitable organization funded entirely by donations|Operating under strict government price controls with continuous treasury subsidies|Operating for profit and achieving financial self-sufficiency without treasury support|Operating exclusively as a regulatory body for private market competitors|Option C|Commercialization mandates that state enterprises operate commercially for profit and attain financial viability independently of government subsidies.
15.1|Which of the following represents a major political or structural risk of asset concentration resulting from rapid privatization?|Excessive decentralization of power to local municipal governments|Undue market dominance by a small group of wealthy elite or foreign investors|Complete democratization of the national economy through broad share distribution|Elimination of all regulatory oversight over corporate governance|Option B|Rapid privatization without robust anti-monopoly frameworks often concentrates valuable national assets in the hands of a wealthy few or foreign entities.
